en: Form is the object of sight and the eye is the seer; that [eye] is an object of sight, but the mental faculty is the seer.
The modifications of the intellect are the objects of sight, while the Witness is indeed the Seer alone and is never itself seen.
Through the distinctions of blue, yellow, gross, subtle, short, long, and so forth,
one may see various kinds of forms with the eye as a single unity.
One should likewise unify the mind regarding the qualities of the eyes, such as blindness, dullness, or sharpness; let this same method be applied to the ears, the skin, and the other senses. (3)
Desire, volition, doubt, faith and lack of faith, steadfastness and its opposite,
shame, intelligence, fear— consciousness illumines these and other such states as one.
This [consciousness] neither rises nor sets; it neither increases nor undergoes diminution.
It shines by itself and, without any external means, illumines all things other than itself.
Due to the entry of the reflection of consciousness (cit), there is an appearance in the intellect (buddhi); however, the intellect exists in two forms:
one is the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti), and the other consists of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
The identity of the shadow and the iron ball is considered to be like that of the reflection and the heated iron mass;
through that identification with the ego (ahaṃkāra), the body attained the state of consciousness.
The identity of the ego with the reflection of consciousness, the body, and the witness is threefold, respectively:
innate, born of karma, and produced by delusion. (8)
When the two related factors exist, there is no cessation of that which is innate;
however, both cease gradually through the exhaustion of karma and through awakening.
In deep sleep, when the ego-sense has dissolved, the body becomes unconscious;
dream occurs during the partial expansion of the ego-sense, while waking is its full expansion. (10)
The modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti), having attained identity with the reflection of consciousness (citicchāyaikya),
projects latent impressions (vāsanās) in a dream, and in the waking state, it perceives external objects through the senses.
The mind, characterized by egoity and grasping, is a single insentient entity that persists through the three states; it is thus born and likewise dies.

For Māyā possesses two powers, consisting of projection (vikṣepa) and concealment (āvṛti). The power of projection creates the universe, from the subtle body (liṅga) up to the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 13 ||
What is called "creation" is the expansion of all names and forms within the reality that is Brahman—being, consciousness, and bliss—like foam and other phenomena upon the ocean. (14)
The lower power veils the distinction between the inner seer and the seen, as well as between Brahman and the world of existence externally; she is the cause of saṃsāra.
Before the witness, the subtle body (liṅga) appears conjoined with the gross body; through the penetration of the reflection of consciousness, it becomes the empirical living being (jīva). || 16 ||
Due to the superimposition of its nature as a living being, this [notion] appears even in the Witness;
however, when the veil has been destroyed and the difference is manifest, that [superimposition] departs.
Likewise, that power which remains concealing the difference between the creation and Brahman, by its influence Brahman appears as if it were modified. (18)
Here too, through the destruction of the veil, the distinction between Brahman and the creation shines forth;
that distinction is a modification belonging to the creation, and never to Brahman.
Existence, luminosity, and loveliness, along with form and name—this is the fivefold division.
The first three constitute the nature of Brahman; the latter two constitute the nature of the world. (20)
In earth, air, fire, water, and earth [the elements], and among gods, animals, humans, and so forth, existence, consciousness, and bliss are undivided; it is only form and name that differ.
Having disregarded both name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and being intent upon the reality of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda),
one should always practice samādhi, whether internally or externally, for the sake of steadfastness.
In the heart, meditative absorption (samādhi) is twofold: with conceptualization (savikalpa) and without conceptualization (nirvikalpa).
That which is with conceptualization is further divided into two types according to its permeation by visible objects or by words. (23)
One should meditate on the conscious Self as the witness of those visible objects—desire and the rest—which reside in the mind;
this samādhi, permeated by the visible, is *savikalpaka* (with conceptualization). || 24 ||

"This am I"—this state, pierced by the word "I," is the conceptual (savikalpaka) samādhi, which is unattached, consisting of existence-consciousness-bliss, self-luminous, and free from duality. || 25 ||
But by entering into the flavor of one's own direct experience, disregarding both the visible and the audible, there arises non-conceptual samādhi, like a lamp placed in a windless spot. (26)
Whether in the heart or in some external object, the first kind of samādhi consists in the separation of name and form from pure existence (sanmātra). || 27 ||
The uninterrupted contemplation that "the reality is an undivided single essence, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss"—this constitutes middling samādhi. (28)
The third [type] is considered to be the state of rigidity resulting from the tasting of aesthetic flavor (rasāsvāda), as previously described.
One should spend time continuously with these six forms of meditative absorption (samādhi).
When the identification with the body has dissolved and the Supreme Self is realized,
wherever the mind goes, there is samādhi.
The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut asunder,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.
The third is the limited reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), which is imagined in the state of dream;
thus the individual soul (jīva) is to be known as threefold, among which the first is the ultimate reality (pāramārthika).
The delimitation would be imagined, whereas that which is delimited is real;
in that [reality], the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) arises through superimposition, while the state of being Brahman exists by its very nature.
The statements such as "That thou art" proclaim the identity of the limited individual soul with the perfect Brahman, and not with any other soul.
Māyā, established in Brahman and consisting of the forms of projection and concealment,
conceals its own indivisibility within that [Brahman] and fashions the world and the individual soul.
The individual soul (jīva), which is the reflection of consciousness residing in the intellect, is indeed the enjoyer and the performer of actions;
this entire world, consisting of the elements and their derivatives, exists as its object of enjoyment.
From beginningless time until prior to liberation, these two remain situated within conventional usage; therefore, both are conventional. (37)

Sleep, which consists of the obscuration of distraction and abides as the reflection of consciousness, covers the world of living beings; having covered it previously, it then projects a new one. (38)
Since these two exist only at the time of their appearance, they are illusory;
for one who has awakened from a dream, those two do not persist in a subsequent dream.
The world belonging to that illusory individual soul (prātibhāsikajīva) is itself illusory;
however, another, the empirical (vyāvahārika) soul, considers it to be real, while [the higher perspective] regards it as false. || 40 ||
That which is the empirical individual soul regards this empirical world as real; however, the absolute [soul] considers it to be false. (41)
The ultimate individual soul, however, realizes its ultimate identity with Brahman;
it perceives nothing else, for it does not perceive through a false nature.
Just as sweetness, fluidity, and coolness—qualities belonging to the cloud—are followed by the wave, and then, following that, are also present in the foam which rests upon it; || 43 ||

Existing as witnesses, being of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss, they follow along through their connection with the empirical world; likewise, they follow through that same door into the illusory world.
When the foam dissolves, its properties such as fluidity and so forth would reside in the wave;
and when that too dissolves, these return to the water just as they were before.
Upon the dissolution of the illusory (prātibhāsika) individual soul, they reside in the empirical (vyāvahārika);
upon its dissolution, they culminate in the Witness, who is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda).
Thus ends the *Dṛgdṛśyaviveka* composed by Tīrthasvāmin Bhāratī.
